title: AI Unlocked: The Humanities
blurb: For writers, historians, linguists, artists, and scholars: research and archival workflows, translation and close-reading at scale, creative collaboration without losing your voice, and the authorship debates every humanist must be able to argue.

modules.d: Why AI is a humanities question as much as a technical one — and what humanists uniquely bring.
modules.body:
AI is built from human culture

Large language models are trained on vast quantities of human writing: books, articles, websites, translations, conversations. Image models learn from human art and photography. In a real sense, generative AI is a compression of human culture — and the humanities, which study that culture, language, meaning and value, are directly implicated. Questions about what these systems "understand", whose voices they represent, what they omit and how they change creativity are humanities questions.

What do language models do?

Language models predict likely sequences of text based on patterns learned from training data. Researchers debate how to describe their capabilities. Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru and colleagues famously described large language models as "stochastic parrots" — producing fluent language without grounded understanding — and warned about bias, environmental cost and the illusion of meaning. Others argue the systems develop useful internal representations. Humanists need not settle this debate to use AI wisely, but they should resist both hype ("it understands everything") and dismissal ("it is just autocomplete"), and judge outputs critically.

Fluency is not truth. Language models can produce elegant prose, confident interpretation and plausible citations that are entirely fabricated. Humanist training — close reading, source criticism, contextual knowledge — is exactly what is needed to detect when fluent text is wrong.

Whose culture? Representation and bias

Training data over-represents widely published languages, cultures and perspectives — especially English and the Global North — and under-represents many African, Indigenous and minority languages and oral traditions. AI outputs can therefore reproduce stereotypes, flatten cultural nuance, or present one tradition's assumptions as universal. Humanists can identify these distortions, contribute better data and descriptions, and advocate for inclusion — for instance through community initiatives building language technology for African languages.

What humanists bring

  • Interpretation: meaning depends on context, genre, history and audience — not just words.
  • Source criticism: evaluating provenance, reliability and bias of evidence.
  • Ethical reasoning: questions of authorship, dignity, representation and responsibility.
  • Language expertise: translation, rhetoric, multilingual nuance.
  • Historical perspective: earlier technologies — printing, photography, the internet — also transformed authorship and knowledge, offering lessons for today.
  • Creativity and voice: the distinctive perspective that makes work worth reading.

Opportunities

AI can accelerate transcription of archives, translation drafts, analysis of large text collections, discovery of patterns across centuries of documents, and creative experimentation. Used critically, it extends the reach of humanistic inquiry. Used uncritically, it produces superficial scholarship and homogenised art.

The stance of this course

We approach AI as humanists: curious, critical, historically informed and ethically serious. The goal is not to defend the humanities against AI, nor to surrender them to it, but to bring humanistic judgement to how AI is used — in research, teaching, translation and art.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my critical discussion partner. I am a [writer/historian/linguist/artist/scholar]. Help me map where AI could help my work and where it could distort it, citing specific risks such as fabrication, cultural bias and loss of voice. Then pose three challenging questions about authorship, representation and meaning that my discipline is particularly well placed to answer.

📚 Glossary

  • Language model: AI system predicting text from learned patterns
  • Stochastic parrots: critique describing LLMs as fluent without grounded understanding
  • Source criticism: evaluating the origin and reliability of evidence
  • Representation bias: over- or under-representation of groups in data and outputs

📖 References

  • Bender, E., Gebru, T. et al. (2021). On the dangers of stochastic parrots: can language models be too big? FAccT.
  • Crawford, K. (2021). Atlas of AI.
  • Masakhane — participatory research on NLP for African languages (masakhane.io).
  • Eisenstein, E. (1979). The Printing Press as an Agent of Change.

modules.d: Transcription, discovery, note-taking and citation — with verification at the core.
modules.body:
Accelerating the research cycle

Humanities research involves finding sources, reading and annotating, transcribing and translating, organising notes, developing arguments and citing accurately. AI can accelerate several steps — but scholarship stands or falls on the accuracy of sources and citations.

Archives and transcription

Many archives contain handwritten letters, administrative records, missionary diaries, colonial reports and community documents that are hard to read and impossible to search. Handwritten text recognition (HTR) platforms such as Transkribus can be trained on samples of a particular hand or script and then transcribe large collections, making them searchable. Optical character recognition (OCR) does the same for printed text. Accuracy varies with script, language and document condition, so transcriptions require sampling and correction before scholarly use.

The fabricated citation problem. General AI chatbots frequently invent references — plausible authors, titles, journals and page numbers that do not exist. A 2023 study in Scientific Reports found that a majority of citations produced by one widely used chatbot model, and a smaller but significant share from a newer model, were fabricated. Never cite a source you have not located and checked yourself.

Discovery and literature review

AI research assistants can suggest search terms, summarise abstracts, map debates and identify gaps. Use them to orient yourself, then go to library catalogues, scholarly databases and the texts themselves. Be aware that AI tools often reflect the most-cited, English-language scholarship and may miss regional journals, African publications and non-digitised sources — exactly where original contributions often lie.

Reading, annotation and notes

AI can summarise long texts, but summaries lose nuance, argumentative structure and the details that matter for interpretation. Use summaries to decide what to read closely, not as substitutes for reading. Reference managers such as Zotero store sources and notes and generate bibliographies in standard styles; keep verified bibliographic data there rather than relying on AI-generated references.

Working with sensitive materials

Archives may contain personal information about living people, sacred or restricted cultural knowledge, or materials governed by copyright or institutional rules. Before uploading documents to AI tools, check archive terms, privacy and copyright, and the wishes of communities connected to the materials. Some knowledge is not meant for public circulation.

Oral history

Speech-to-text tools can transcribe interviews quickly, but quality varies by language, accent and recording conditions, and transcription is itself interpretive — choices about punctuation, dialect and silence shape meaning. Obtain informed consent for recording, transcription and any use of AI tools; return transcripts to interviewees where appropriate; and follow oral history ethics.

A verified research workflow

  1. Use AI to brainstorm questions and search terms.
  2. Find sources through catalogues, databases and archives.
  3. Verify every source exists and says what you think it says.
  4. Use AI to transcribe, translate drafts or summarise — then check.
  5. Write your argument in your own words, with your own interpretation.
  6. Cite from your reference manager, and disclose AI use as required by your institution or publisher.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my research assistant for a humanities project on [topic]. Suggest 15 search terms in English and French, key debates I should explore, and types of archives and databases to consult, including African and regional sources. Do NOT invent citations — instead tell me what kinds of sources to look for. Then design a verification checklist for any transcription or translation I produce with AI.

📚 Glossary

  • HTR: handwritten text recognition
  • OCR: optical character recognition for printed text
  • Transkribus: platform for transcribing historical documents with HTR
  • Reference manager: software storing sources and generating citations, e.g., Zotero
  • Oral history: recorded interviews preserving personal and community memory

📖 References

  • Walters, W. & Wilder, E. (2023). Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT. Scientific Reports.
  • READ-COOP — Transkribus documentation.
  • Oral History Association — Principles and Best Practices.
  • Zotero documentation (zotero.org).

modules.d: Machine translation, multilingual scholarship, and the difference between close and distant reading.
modules.body:
Translation is interpretation

Every translation makes choices: tone, register, cultural references, wordplay, rhythm, ambiguity. Machine translation (MT) and large language models now produce fluent drafts between many languages, transforming everyday multilingual work. For humanists, the question is not whether AI translates, but how to use it without losing what matters.

What machine translation does well — and poorly

Modern MT performs best between widely represented languages and for straightforward informational text. It struggles with literary style, irony, idioms, culturally specific concepts, archaic language, dialects, code-switching and low-resource languages — including many African languages. It may also produce smooth but wrong translations, quietly normalising unusual phrasing that carries meaning.

Domestication and foreignisation. Translation theorist Lawrence Venuti distinguished domesticating translation, which makes a text read smoothly in the target culture, from foreignising translation, which preserves the foreignness of the original. Machine translation tends to domesticate — producing fluent, familiar prose that can erase cultural difference. Humanists must decide deliberately which approach serves the text and readers.

A professional AI-assisted translation workflow

  1. Understand the source: genre, purpose, audience, cultural context.
  2. Machine draft: generate a first draft, possibly from more than one system to compare.
  3. Post-edit: revise for accuracy, register, terminology and style — line by line against the source.
  4. Check culture-specific elements: proverbs, names, forms of address, religious or legal terms.
  5. Review: ideally by a second fluent reader; for publication, by a qualified translator.
  6. Disclose: state how translation was produced where academic or publishing norms require it.

In bilingual contexts such as Cameroon — English and French, alongside many national languages and Cameroonian Pidgin English — translation is everyday civic and scholarly work. AI can speed it up, but terms with legal, religious or cultural weight need human expertise.

Close reading in an AI age

Close reading — attentive analysis of language, form, imagery and structure — remains the core of literary and textual interpretation. AI can support it: identifying rhetorical devices, tracking motifs, comparing translations, or generating counter-readings to test your interpretation. But AI interpretations are generalised; your reading must engage the specific text, its history and its critical conversation.

Distant reading and text analysis

Franco Moretti proposed distant reading: studying large numbers of texts computationally to see patterns invisible to individual reading — genre change, vocabulary shifts, networks of characters. Text analysis tools (word frequencies, topic modelling, named entity recognition) and AI can analyse whole archives or literatures. The insight comes from combining distant patterns with close interpretation: numbers raise questions that reading answers.

Language technology for African languages

Communities of researchers, including the Masakhane initiative, are building datasets and models for African languages, often participatory and community-led. Humanists — linguists, translators, writers — are essential contributors, ensuring that language technology respects grammar, culture and speakers' priorities.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my translation editor. I will paste a short source passage and a machine translation. Compare them line by line, identify errors in meaning, register, idiom and culturally specific terms, explain whether the translation domesticates or foreignises, and propose a revised translation with notes on each choice. Flag terms that need an expert or native-speaker check.

📚 Glossary

  • Machine translation: automatic translation by software
  • Post-editing: human revision of machine-translated text
  • Domestication / foreignisation: making a translation familiar versus preserving its foreignness
  • Close reading: attentive analysis of a text's language and form
  • Distant reading: computational analysis of many texts to find patterns

📖 References

  • Venuti, L. (1995). The Translator's Invisibility.
  • Moretti, F. (2013). Distant Reading.
  • Masakhane (masakhane.io) — African languages NLP research.
  • ISO 18587:2017 — Post-editing of machine translation output.

modules.t: Creative Collaboration Without Losing Your Voice
modules.d: Using AI in writing and art as a collaborator — while protecting originality, voice and craft.
modules.body:
The creative question

Writers, poets, visual artists, musicians and filmmakers face a new kind of collaborator: a system that can generate text, images and sound instantly. Some artists refuse it; some embrace it; many experiment cautiously. The central question is not whether to use AI, but how to use it while keeping what makes your work yours — your voice, perspective, craft and integrity.

Modes of collaboration

  • Brainstorming partner: generating many possibilities you then select from, reject or transform.
  • Critic and editor: asking for feedback on clarity, pacing or structure — you decide what to change.
  • Research assistant: background on settings, periods, techniques — verified independently.
  • Constraint generator: prompts, forms or rules that push you out of habits.
  • Material: some artists work with AI outputs deliberately as raw material, exploring the technology itself as subject.
  • Production support: formatting, transcription, translation drafts, accessibility versions.
The voice test. After working with AI, read your piece aloud or view it alongside your earlier work. Does it sound like you? Would readers who know your work recognise it? If AI phrasing, imagery or rhythm has replaced your own, revise until your voice returns. Generic AI style — predictable metaphors, balanced triplets, smooth but empty phrases — is easy to spot and erodes distinctiveness.

Protecting craft and growth

Creative skill develops through struggle: drafting badly, revising, finding solutions. Outsourcing that struggle can stunt growth, especially for emerging writers and artists. A useful practice: write or draft first yourself, then use AI for critique or alternatives — rather than starting from AI output. Keep notebooks and drafts that show your process.

Honesty and disclosure

Audiences, publishers, competitions and grant bodies increasingly have policies on AI use. Some prohibit AI-generated content; others require disclosure; some magazines have closed submissions after floods of AI-generated stories. Read submission guidelines and disclose accurately. Presenting AI-generated work as entirely your own where that matters to others is a form of deception.

Respecting other artists

Prompting AI to imitate a living artist's distinctive style or to produce work "in the style of" a named illustrator raises ethical concerns and, in some contexts, legal ones. Many artists object to their work being used to train models without consent or compensation. Consider credit, consent and the effect of your practice on fellow artists' livelihoods.

African and diaspora creativity

AI tools trained predominantly on Western data may default to Western aesthetics, names, settings and narrative structures. African and diaspora artists can push against these defaults, insist on cultural specificity, and use their own archives, languages and forms. Your perspective is precisely what generic systems lack.

Documenting your process

Keep records of how you used AI — prompts, outputs, and how you transformed them. This supports honest disclosure, potential copyright claims based on human contribution, and your own reflection on what helped and what did not.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my creative critic, not my ghostwriter. I will paste a draft I wrote myself. Give me specific feedback on voice, imagery, pacing and structure, point out any passages that sound generic, and ask me three questions that push the piece deeper. Do not rewrite the piece; suggest at most two alternative lines as examples of a direction, which I will rework in my own words.

📚 Glossary

  • Voice: an artist's distinctive style and perspective
  • Constraint: a rule or limit used to stimulate creativity
  • Disclosure: stating how AI was used in creating work
  • Style imitation: producing work mimicking a specific artist's distinctive style

📖 References

  • Clarkesworld Magazine (2023) — statement on closing submissions due to AI-generated stories.
  • Society of Authors / Authors Guild — guidance on AI and authors.
  • Chiang, T. (2023). Will A.I. become the new McKinsey? / ChatGPT is a blurry JPEG of the web. The New Yorker.

quiz.x: Constraints can stimulate creativity.

modules.d: Copyright, training data, academic integrity and what originality means now.
modules.body:
Old questions, new urgency

What makes someone an author? What counts as original? Who owns a creative work? Humanists have debated these questions for centuries — from medieval scribes and collaborative workshops to Barthes's "death of the author" and the remix culture of the internet. Generative AI gives them new urgency and legal consequences.

Copyright and human authorship

In many legal systems, copyright protects works of human authorship. In the United States, the Copyright Office has refused registration for material generated by AI without sufficient human creative control, and in Thaler v. Perlmutter the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. affirmed in 2025 that a work created autonomously by an AI system cannot be registered because human authorship is required. Human selection, arrangement and modification of AI material can be protected. Other countries take different approaches, and law is evolving — creators should check their jurisdiction.

Training data and fair use debates

AI systems are trained on vast collections of books, articles, images and music, often without explicit permission from creators. Authors, news organisations, artists and record labels have brought lawsuits in several countries — for example authors' and news publishers' cases against AI companies in the United States. Early court rulings have been mixed and many cases remain ongoing; some disputes have moved toward licensing agreements. The debate involves copyright, fair use or fair dealing, compensation and consent, and the future economics of creative work.

Academic integrity. Universities, journals and publishers have issued AI policies. Publication ethics bodies such as COPE state that AI tools cannot be listed as authors because they cannot take responsibility for the work; authors must disclose AI use and remain accountable for accuracy. Style guides such as MLA and APA provide formats for citing AI-generated content. Always follow your institution's and venue's specific rules.

What is originality now?

Originality has never meant creation from nothing; all work draws on tradition. In an AI age, originality increasingly lies in judgement (what to ask, select and reject), perspective (lived experience and situated knowledge), argument (new interpretations supported by evidence), form (distinctive structures and styles), and access (sources, communities and experiences others cannot reach). These are human contributions that AI cannot supply by itself.

Detecting AI use — and its limits

Educators sometimes rely on AI-detection software. Research and experience show these tools produce false positives and negatives, and some studies have found they disproportionately flag non-native English writers. Detection scores should never be the sole basis for accusations. Better approaches include assessment design (process, drafts, oral defence, personal reflection), clear policies and conversation.

Teaching the humanities with AI

Humanities educators can teach students to use AI critically: comparing AI interpretations with their own, identifying fabricated sources, analysing AI bias, and reflecting on authorship. Assignments that require personal voice, local sources, archival work and in-class discussion remain meaningful and resistant to outsourcing.

Your position

Humanists will disagree about AI, and that diversity is healthy. What matters is that positions are informed, transparent and consistent with professional ethics: honesty about how work is produced, respect for other creators, and accountability for what we publish.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my debate partner on AI and authorship. Present the strongest arguments on both sides of three questions: (1) Should AI-generated works receive copyright? (2) Is training AI on copyrighted works without permission fair? (3) Should students be allowed to use AI in humanities essays? Then help me draft a short, reasoned position statement for my discipline, noting where law varies by jurisdiction.

📚 Glossary

  • Human authorship: human creative contribution required for copyright in many jurisdictions
  • Fair use / fair dealing: legal doctrines allowing limited use of copyrighted material
  • COPE: Committee on Publication Ethics
  • False positive: incorrectly flagging human work as AI-generated
  • Originality: distinctive contribution of judgement, perspective, argument or form

📖 References

  • Thaler v. Perlmutter, U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (2025).
  • U.S. Copyright Office (2025). Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability.
  • COPE (2023). Authorship and AI tools — position statement.
  • Liang, W. et al. (2023). GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers. Patterns.
  • MLA and APA style guidance on citing generative AI.

modules.t: Capstone: A Work of AI-Assisted Scholarship or Art
modules.d: Produce and reflect on a scholarly or creative work that uses AI critically and transparently.
modules.body:
Your capstone

Create a work of AI-assisted scholarship or art in your discipline — a research essay, archival project, translation, digital exhibition, short story collection, poetry sequence, artwork series, or teaching unit — accompanied by a critical reflection on how AI was used.

Options

  • Archival project: transcribe and analyse a small collection using HTR or OCR, with verified transcriptions and an interpretive essay.
  • Translation project: translate a text using a machine draft and post-editing, with a translator's note explaining your choices.
  • Distant and close reading: analyse a corpus computationally and interpret the patterns through close reading.
  • Creative work: produce writing or art using AI in a defined collaborative mode, documenting your process and voice.
  • Teaching unit: design lessons that teach students to use and critique AI in a humanities subject.

Requirements

  1. The work itself, of a quality appropriate to your field.
  2. Process documentation: prompts, AI outputs and your transformations or corrections, with dates.
  3. Verification record: how you checked sources, transcriptions, translations or facts.
  4. Ethics statement: consent, copyright, cultural sensitivity and privacy considerations.
  5. Disclosure statement in the form your field would expect (e.g., MLA/APA citation or a creator's note).
  6. Critical reflection (800–1,200 words): what AI contributed, what it distorted or could not do, how your voice and judgement shaped the work, and what this suggests about your discipline's future.
Assessment criteria. Quality and originality of the work; rigour of verification; ethical and cultural responsibility; transparency of process; and depth of critical reflection. A modest project done with integrity and insight is stronger than an ambitious one done carelessly.

Sharing your work

Consider sharing your capstone with your cohort, community or institution. Humanistic engagement with AI is still being defined — your work contributes to that conversation.

  • Verification record: evidence of checks on sources and outputs
  • Ethics statement: account of consent, rights and sensitivity considerations
  • Critical reflection: analysis of what AI contributed and distorted
